description: ARKS Terra is a team of passionate students from Abdul Rahman Kanoo School Diyar, Bahrain, dedicated to combining technology, innovation, and Earth science. Participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, we aim to develop creative solutions using NASA's open data, artificial intelligence, and interactive visualizations to explore environmental trends, understand our changing planet, and make scientific discoveries more accessible to everyone.
summary: EarthLens is an interactive web app that turns NASA Earth observation data into clear, tested climate trends. You pick a place on a 3D globe, starting from Bahrain, or search for anywhere on Earth. EarthLens then pulls real monthly NASA data for surface skin temperature and precipitation (MERRA-2 via NASA POWER) and daytime land surface temperature (Terra MODIS MOD11A2). It plots the time series and runs a seasonal Mann–Kendall test with Sen's slope in Python. That tells you whether a trend is statistically significant and how fast it is changing per decade. Users can compare two locations, average over a regional box, and download a fully documented CSV. An optional AI guide explains the results in plain English, but every number comes from Python, never the AI. This answers the Trend Detective challenge: what is changing, where, how fast, and how confident we can be. It matters because global averages hide local change. Gulf countries like Bahrain face extreme heat and water stress, and EarthLens lets students, teachers and the public check the evidence for their own region.
details:
What it does: EarthLens is a climate trend explorer. The user picks a location (Manama, an Arabian Gulf offshore point, a 2° Bahrain area box, or any place found by name or latitude/longitude) and a variable. EarthLens fetches the real monthly NASA data on demand, shows it on an interactive chart with a 12-month mean, and reports the trend's direction, its rate per decade, and whether it is statistically significant.

How it works:

  • Data: NASA POWER monthly MERRA-2 surface skin temperature (TS) and corrected precipitation (PRECTOTCORR), plus Terra MODIS MOD11A2.061 daytime land surface temperature (LST_Day_1km) through Microsoft Planetary Computer's public STAC API.
  • MODIS processing: Kelvin-to-°C conversion, two quality modes (Exploratory and Strict) based on the QC_Day bits, and 8-day composites weighted into calendar months. Partial final years are dropped so they don't skew the trend.
  • Statistics: a two-sided seasonal Mann–Kendall test with tie correction, plus a seasonal Sen's slope in units per decade, at p < 0.05. Months are compared like-for-like (January with January), so the annual cycle isn't mistaken for a climate trend.
  • Comparison: a second location's series can be overlaid, and a regional box gives a cosine-latitude-weighted area mean.
  • 3D globe: an interactive Earth using NASA Blue Marble imagery, centred on the selected point.
  • Export: a self-describing CSV with units, coordinates, product, source links, sampling notes and MODIS quality fields.
  • AI guide (optional): DeepSeek explains the computed results and answers follow-up questions. It only receives the Python-computed statistics, and the app works fully without it.

Benefits and impact: EarthLens makes NASA data usable for people who aren't scientists. It shows that change is local and uneven, and it is honest about uncertainty. It labels lower-quality MODIS data, explains that point samples are not national averages, and notes that significance doesn't prove a cause. We built it with Bahrain as home base so students and the public in the Gulf can investigate their own climate, but it works anywhere on Earth.

Tools: Python, Streamlit, pandas, Plotly, requests, Globe.GL and three.js, NASA POWER API, Microsoft Planetary Computer, OpenStreetMap Nominatim, the DeepSeek API, GitHub, and pytest (50 automated tests).

Creativity and factors considered: we combined a 3D globe, real-time NASA data and rigorous seasonal statistics with a plain-English AI explainer, while keeping the AI away from the numbers. We considered data quality, the difference between reanalysis data and satellite data, seasonality, autocorrelation limits, honest labelling, fair use of the place-search service, and keeping API keys out of the code.

Use of Super Intelligence (SI): All images in our presentation were generated with ChatGPT (OpenAI) and are watermarked as SI-generated. SI coding assistants helped write and debug parts of the code, and every part was reviewed and tested by our team (50 automated tests). SI also helped draft and edit written text such as this description. Inside the app, the optional DeepSeek AI guide writes plain-English explanations of the results; all statistics are calculated in Python, not by the AI. No NASA logos or branding were generated or modified.
